brief: Nobles 1..n have power i, friendships form an undirected graph. A noble is vulnerable if it has a friend and all friends are stronger; vulnerable nobles die simultaneously and repeatedly until none remain. Given add/remove edge queries and count-survivor queries, print the survivors for each type-3 query.
key_idea: Noble i dies iff it has a friend with higher power and every lower-power friend has already died; process nodes in increasing order of power.
solution: 1. Let dead[i] = (i has some friend j > i) AND (every friend j < i has dead[j] = true).
2. Compute dead[] for i = 1..n in increasing order, since dead[i] only depends on smaller indices.
3. Survivors = number of i with dead[i] = false (isolated nobles and nobles with only weaker friends survive).
4. Maintain adjacency sets under type-1 and type-2 queries; on each type-3 query recompute survivors.
5. Edge case: a noble whose only friends are weaker is never vulnerable and survives.
complexity: O(q * (n + m)) time with the recomputation below, O(n + m) space; a faster dynamic solution is needed for the full limits
dry_run: Sample 1, edges 2-1, 1-3, 3-4, first query 3: dead[1]=T (friends 2,3 higher); dead[2]=F (only friend 1 is lower); dead[3]=T (higher friend 4, lower friend 1 dead); dead[4]=F (only lower friend 3).
Survivors {2,4}, prints 2. Queries 1 2 3 (add 2-3) and 2 3 1 (remove 3-1) give edges 2-1, 3-4, 2-3.
Second query 3: dead[1]=T (higher friend 2); dead[2]=T (higher friend 3, lower friend 1 dead); dead[3]=T (higher friend 4, lower friend 2 dead); dead[4]=F. Survivors = 1, matching the sample.

brief: Given an array a, its GCD-sequence b_i = gcd(a_i, a_{i+1}). Decide whether removing exactly one element makes the GCD-sequence non-decreasing.
key_idea: Find the first index p where b_p > b_{p+1}; the removed element must be a_p, a_{p+1} or a_{p+2}, so test only those three.
solution: 1. Compute gcd of adjacent pairs and find the first p with gcd(a_p, a_{p+1}) > gcd(a_{p+1}, a_{p+2}) (0-based).
2. If no such p exists, the answer is YES (already non-decreasing; removing any element keeps it valid, so YES).
3. Otherwise, any removed index outside {p, p+1, p+2} keeps the pair b_p, b_{p+1} adjacent and violated, so only those 3 candidates matter.
4. For each candidate k in {p, p+1, p+2} that exists, build the array without a_k and check its GCD-sequence in O(n).
5. Print YES if any candidate works, else NO. Edge: the removed element may be the first or last, which just drops one GCD term.
complexity: O(n log A) time per test (A = 1e9, gcd cost), O(n) space; sum of n is 2e5
dry_run: Sample a = 12 6 3 4 (expected NO): b = [6,3,1], first violation p=0 (6 > 3), candidates remove index 0,1,2.
Remove a_0: [6,3,4] gives b = [3,1], decreasing, fail.
Remove a_1: [12,3,4] gives b = [3,1], fail. Remove a_2: [12,6,4] gives b = [6,2], fail.
Result NO, matching the sample.

brief: An n x m grid has a monotone path from (1,1) to (n,m) (moves D or R) whose cells were set to 0. Refill the path cells with integers so every row and every column has the same sum; off-path cells are unchanged and any valid answer is accepted.
key_idea: Target common sum 0. Walk the path: when leaving a row by moving D, set the current cell to cancel that row; when leaving a column by moving R, cancel that column; the last cell cancels its row, and the total-sum argument forces its column to 0 too.
solution: 1. Compute row sums rs[] and column sums cs[] of the grid (path cells are 0).
2. Walk the path string from (1,1). At cell (i,j), if the next step is D, set value v = -rs[i]; if R, set v = -cs[j].
3. Add v to the cell, rs[i], and cs[j]; then move (i+1,j) for D or (i,j+1) for R.
4. At the final cell (n,m) set v = -rs[n] (last row) and update; column m then sums to 0 because total sum is 0.
5. Print the grid; values stay within about 1e9 so use long long.
complexity: O(n*m) time and space per test; sum of n*m is 1e6
dry_run: Own example: n=2, m=2, s=DR, off-path cell (1,2)=3, path cells (1,1),(2,1),(2,2) are 0.
Final (2,2): v=-rs[2]=-3, cell(2,2)=-3. Grid [[-3,3],[3,-3]], all row and column sums are 0.

brief: Sasha has a coins and bets repeatedly: a win pays y*k back and a loss costs y; he never loses more than x times in a row. Decide whether he can guarantee winnings of any size.
key_idea: Not determined: the fetched text was a paraphrase, and a simple strategy analysis (bet 1 during losses, bet the rest on the forced win) predicts YES for sample cases 4 and 7 where the expected answer is NO, so the exact rule is unverified.
solution: 1. Read the statement again from the official page; the paraphrase omitted exact rules about bet sizes and when a forced win occurs.
2. Verify any candidate formula against all 9 sample answers before trusting it.
3. Do not rely on the unverified strategy analysis in key_idea.
4. Only after confirming the rule, derive the threshold on a and k, x.
complexity: O(t) per test once the formula is known
dry_run: Sample case k=3, x=3, a=6 (expected NO): the naive strategy predicts YES, so the rule is not yet confirmed.
No own example is given because the rule is unverified.

brief: Given a binary string s, f(s) sums each adjacent pair read as a two-digit number. Using at most k adjacent swaps, minimize f(s).
key_idea: f(s) = 11*cnt - 10*[last char is 1] - [first char is 1], so greedily move the last 1 to the end if affordable (worth 10), then the first 1 to the front if affordable (worth 1).
solution: 1. Let cnt be the number of ones. If cnt = 0, answer is 0.
2. Start from ans = 11*cnt.
3. Let p be the 0-based index of the last 1; cost to move it to the end is (n-1) - p. If cost <= k, subtract 10 and reduce k by cost.
4. Let q be the 0-based index of the first 1; cost to move it to the front is q. If (cnt >= 2 or the end move was not done) and q <= k, subtract 1.
5. Edge case: with cnt = 1 the same one cannot serve both ends, so only one bonus is possible.
complexity: O(n) time, O(n) space per test; sum of n is 1e5
dry_run: Sample 3: n=5, k=2, s=00110. ones at indices 2,3, cnt=2, ans=22.
Last one p=3, cost (4-3)=1 <= 2, so ans=12 and k=1.
First one q=2, cost 2 > 1, so no further change. Output 12, matching the sample.

brief: Given a multiset of plank lengths that changes by single additions and removals, after each event decide whether two storages can be built: one square and one rectangle, each using four planks of matching sides.
key_idea: Maintain pairs = sum of floor(cnt[x]/2) and quad = number of lengths with cnt[x] >= 4; the answer is YES iff pairs >= 4 and quad >= 1.
solution: 1. Keep cnt[x] for each plank length x, up to 1e5.
2. Maintain pairs = sum over x of cnt[x]/2 and quad = number of x with cnt[x] >= 4, updating both in O(1) per event.
3. The square needs 4 planks of one length (2 pairs of x), the rectangle needs 2 more pairs of any lengths.
4. So the answer is YES iff quad >= 1 and pairs >= 4.
5. Edge case: if the same length gives both square and rectangle pairs, the count still works because the square takes 2 pairs from a length with cnt >= 4.
complexity: O((n + q)) time, O(max x) space
dry_run: Sample: initial 1 1 1 2 1 1 gives cnt1=5, cnt2=1, pairs=2, quad=1.
+2: cnt2=2, pairs=3, answer NO (pairs < 4).
+1: cnt1=6, pairs=4, quad=1, answer YES.
-1: cnt1=5, pairs=3, answer NO, matching the sample NO YES NO.

brief: Alice and Bob play Everything Nim on n piles: a move picks k no larger than the smallest nonempty pile and removes k from every nonempty pile; the player unable to move loses. Print the winner under optimal play for each test.
key_idea: Sort the distinct values and take layer differences d_i = v_i - v_{i-1} from the bottom; scanning from the top, F = (not F) or (d_i >= 2), and Alice wins iff the final F is true.
solution: 1. Sort the piles and remove duplicates, giving distinct values v_1 < ... < v_m.
2. Set d_i = v_i - v_{i-1} with v_0 = 0; a move only shrinks the bottom layer, and each layer behaves as a heap where a player can take any amount.
3. Let f(R) be whether the player to move wins on the layers above a state. Derived rule: f(h, R) is true iff f(R) is false, or h >= 2 when f(R) is true.
4. Start from the top layer with F = false (empty suffix), and for i = m down to 1 set F = (not F) or (d_i >= 2).
5. Print Alice if F is true else Bob. The rule was checked against all seven sample cases.
complexity: O(n log n) time per test, O(n) space; sum of n is 2e5
dry_run: Sample pile 2 1 3 4 2 4: distinct sorted values 1 2 3 4, layer differences d = 1 1 1 1.
i=4 (d=1): F = (not false) or false = true.
i=3 (d=1): F = (not true) or false = false. i=2: F = true. i=1: F = false.
Final F = false, print Bob, matching the sample.

brief: Given a, b, r (up to 1e18), choose x with 0 <= x <= r to minimize |(a XOR x) - (b XOR x)|, and print the minimum value.
key_idea: Only bits where a and b differ matter; each such bit contributes +-2^i depending on x. Fix the sign of the top differing bit, then greedily give lower differing bits the opposite sign while x stays <= r (tracking whether x is still equal to r's prefix).
solution: 1. Find the highest bit T where a and b differ. If none, the answer is 0.
2. Try both signs sg in {+1, -1} for the top differing bit; skip a sign if it forces x above r at bit T.
3. Walk bits from T down to 0 with a flag tight (x prefix equals r prefix). Non-differing bits take x_i = 0.
4. For a differing bit, prefer sign -sg; set x_i accordingly, and if tight and x_i > r_i flip to the other sign (possible because it is then 0). If x_i < r_i, tight becomes false.
5. Accumulate D = sum of signed 2^i and take the minimum of |D| over the two signs.
complexity: O(60) time per test, O(1) space
dry_run: Sample a=0 b=3 r=2 (expected 1): differing bits 1 and 0, T=1.
sg=+1: bit1 gives x=1 (<= r bit 1), D=+2, still tight; bit0 prefers -1 with x=0, D=2-1=1.
sg=-1 path: bit1 gives x=0 (loose), D=-2; bit0 prefers +1, D=-1. Minimum |D| = 1, matching the sample.

brief: Given an array a of non-negative integers with values at most n, repeatedly take a prefix and append its MEX to b, removing it; choose prefixes to make b lexicographically maximum, then print its length and elements.
key_idea: Always take the shortest prefix whose MEX equals the MEX of the remaining suffix (mex of the suffix is precomputed right to left); if that suffix MEX is 0, take single elements.
solution: 1. Precompute sm[i] = mex of a[i..n-1] by scanning from the right and adding values; the mex never decreases.
2. At position i, let M = sm[i]. If M = 0, append 0 and move to i+1.
3. Otherwise scan forward from i until all values 0..M-1 have appeared (use a stamp array to count distinct values below M), and append M.
4. Continue from the index after that prefix; the total scanning is O(n) because segments are disjoint.
5. Print the length of b, then its elements on one line.
complexity: O(n) time per test, O(n) space; sum of n is 2e5
dry_run: Sample 2 2 3 4 0 1 2 0: sm[0]=5, scan to index 5 (prefix 2 2 3 4 0 1 has 0..4), append 5.
Remaining 2 0: sm=1, prefix 2 0 contains 0, append 1.
b = [5, 1], length 2, matching the sample.

brief: Petya has n dishes from n restaurants. Each can be delivered by courier (time a_i, all couriers start together) or picked up himself (time b_i, pickups add up). Choose the split that minimizes the total time until all dishes are home.
key_idea: Sort by courier time a ascending; the courier set should be a prefix, and the rest is self-picked, giving min over prefixes of max(a of last courier item, sum of b over the rest).
solution: 1. Sort the pairs (a_i, b_i) by a ascending.
2. Compute suffix sums suf[i] = sum of b over indices i..n-1.
3. Candidate for courier prefix of length i: max(a[i-1], suf[i]), with i = 0 giving suf[0] (everything picked up).
4. Take the minimum over i = 0..n.
5. Edge case: ties in a do not matter because the prefix max is the last element's a.
complexity: O(n log n) time per test, O(n) space; sum of n is 2e5
dry_run: Minimum 5, matching the sample.

brief: Given an array of n positive integers, you may reorder it. The beauty is min(LIS(a), LIS(reversed a)) using strictly increasing subsequences. Print the maximum beauty.
key_idea: Answer = min(number of distinct values, (n+1)/2). Each value can appear at most once in each strictly increasing run, and an increasing and a decreasing subsequence share at most one element, so their lengths sum to at most n+1.
solution: 1. Count the number of distinct values D.
2. Upper bounds: any strictly increasing subsequence uses distinct values, so beauty <= D; and LIS(a) + LIS(reversed a) <= n + 1 gives beauty <= (n+1)/2.
3. The bound is attained by an arrangement that puts distinct values in a zigzag pattern of the right length.
4. Print min(D, (n+1)/2) (integer division).
5. Edge case: n = 1 gives min(1, 1) = 1.
complexity: O(n log n) time per test (sort), O(n) space; sum of n is 2e5
dry_run: Sample 2 5 4 5 2 4 (n=6): distinct values {2,4,5} so D=3.
(n+1)/2 = 3, so answer min(3,3) = 3, matching the sample.
Sample 1 6 6 6 (n=3): D=1, (3+1)/2=2, answer 1, matching the sample.

brief: Given k colors and an array, paint some elements, each with one color in 1..k, so that equal-valued elements never share a color, every color is used the same number of times, and the number of painted elements is maximum. Output a coloring (0 = unpainted).
key_idea: Each value can contribute at most min(freq, k) painted elements. Lay out up to k occurrences of each value consecutively, and color position p with (p mod k)+1 for the first c*k positions, where c = total/k.
solution: 1. Group equal values together (sort indices by value).
2. For each value, take its first min(freq, k) indices and append them to a list L in group order.
3. Let c = |L| / k (integer division). The maximum painted count is c*k, because each value can supply at most min(freq,k) and the total must be a multiple of k.
4. Color L[p] with (p mod k) + 1 for p < c*k; every other element stays 0.
5. Same-value elements sit in one block of length <= k, so their positions have distinct residues mod k and hence different colors.
complexity: O(n log n) time per test, O(n) space; sum of n is 2e5
dry_run: Sample 2: n=4, k=4, values 1 1 1 1. Group of value 1 has 4 occurrences, so L = [0,1,2,3] (indices), c = 1.
Colors: index0->1, index1->2, index2->3, index3->4.
Output 1 2 3 4 paints 4 elements with distinct colors, matching the maximum 4 (any valid coloring is accepted).

brief: An n x m grid and w gorillas with heights, each in a distinct cell. The spectacle is the sum over all k x k sub-squares of the total height inside. Maximize the spectacle over placements.
key_idea: A cell's coverage is the number of k x k windows containing it, equal to rowCover(i) * colCover(j). Pair the largest heights with the largest coverages (rearrangement inequality).
solution: 1. For row i, rowCover(i) = min(i, n-k) - max(0, i-k+1) + 1; similarly colCover(j) for columns with m.
2. Build the coverage value rowCover(i)*colCover(j) for all n*m cells.
3. Sort coverage values descending and heights descending.
4. Answer = sum over t < w of height[t] * coverage[t]; the rest of the cells stay empty.
5. Use 64-bit integers: the total can reach about 2.5e18.
complexity: O(nm log(nm) + w log w) time per test, O(nm) space; sum of n*m is 2e5
dry_run: Sample 1: n=3, m=4, k=2, w=9 with all heights 1. Row coverages are 1,2,1; column coverages are 1,2,2,1.
Cell coverages sorted: 4,4, then six 2s, then the rest (1s). Top 9 values: 4+4+2*6+1 = 21.
Output 21, matching the sample.

brief: Three carvers each choose one integer pattern in [1, 1e9]. Given n requested patterns a_i, each request is served by a carver and waits |x - a_i|. Minimize the maximum waiting time.
key_idea: Binary search the answer T; a carver with pattern x can serve exactly the values in [x-T, x+T], so check whether the sorted values can be covered by at most 3 windows of length 2T by greedy left-to-right covering.
solution: 1. Sort a ascending.
2. For a candidate T, greedily start a window at the smallest uncovered value a[i] and cover all values <= a[i] + 2T.
3. T is feasible if the number of windows is at most 3.
4. Binary search the smallest feasible T in [0, 1e9].
5. Edge case: n = 1 or 2 is always feasible at T = 0 (each value gets its own carver).
complexity: O(n log n + n log C) time per test with C = 1e9, O(n) space
dry_run: Sample 2: values sorted 1 2 4 5 30 60. T=1: windows [1,3],[4,6],[30,32],[60,62] need 4 windows, infeasible.
T=2: windows [1,5],[30,34],[60,64] need 3 windows, feasible.
Answer 2, matching the sample.

brief: Mocha and Diana each have a forest on nodes 1..n. Find the maximum set of new edges that can be added to both forests so that both remain forests, and print one such set.
key_idea: A simple greedy over all pairs (add (u,v) when u and v are in different components in both DSUs) gives a maximal set, but whether it is maximum is not verified here; the maximum needs matroid-intersection style reasoning, so no code is given.
solution: 1. Build two DSUs from Mocha's and Diana's initial edges.
2. For each pair u < v, if find1(u) != find1(v) and find2(u) != find2(v), add (u,v) and union in both DSUs.
3. Print the count and the chosen pairs.
4. Sample 3 with this greedy gives 5 added edges, matching the sample count.
5. Caveat: a maximal set is not always maximum for two matroids, so the greedy's optimality is unproven here.
complexity: O(n^2 * alpha(n)) time for the greedy, O(n) space; n <= 1000
dry_run: Sample 2 (n=5, Mocha 5-4,2-1,4-3; Diana 4-3,1-4): pair (1,2) rejected by DSU1, (1,3) and (1,4) rejected by DSU2, (1,5) is accepted by both DSUs.
Greedy gives count 1 with (1,5), which matches the count 1 of the sample (any valid pair is accepted).
Later pairs such as (2,4) are rejected because after (1,5) they would create a cycle.

brief: Given n days, a visit length d, and k job intervals [l_i, r_i], pick a start day for the brother (maximizing the number of distinct jobs overlapping the d-day visit) and one for the mother (minimizing it), choosing the earliest start on ties.
key_idea: Job [l,r] overlaps a visit starting at s iff s is in [l-d+1, r] (clipped to [1, n-d+1]); add +1/-1 on a difference array over starts, then take the earliest max and earliest min.
solution: 1. Starts range over s in [1, n-d+1]. Let S = n-d+1.
2. For each job, lo = max(1, l-d+1), hi = min(r, S); if lo <= hi, add 1 at lo and subtract 1 at hi+1 in a difference array.
3. Prefix-sum the difference array to get the overlap count for each start s.
4. Brother: earliest s with the maximum count (update only on strictly greater). Mother: earliest s with the minimum count (update only on strictly smaller).
5. Edge case: d = n gives a single start, so both answers are 1.
complexity: O(n + k) time per test, O(n) space; sum of n is 2e5
dry_run: Sample 2: n=4, d=1, jobs [1,2] and [2,4]. Starts 1..4 get counts 1, 2, 1, 1.
Brother: earliest maximum is start 2. Mother: earliest minimum is start 1.
Output 2 1, matching the sample.

brief: A drone starts at height 0 and passes n obstacles, where obstacle i requires height in [l_i, r_i]. Each step changes height by d_i in {0, 1}, with some d_i given and others (-1) unknown. Fill the unknowns so every obstacle is passed, or print -1.
key_idea: Track the set of reachable heights after each obstacle as an interval [lo, hi]: a fixed step shifts it, an unknown step widens it to [lo, hi+1], then intersect with [l_i, r_i]; backtrack from a final height to recover the steps.
solution: 1. Set R_0 = [0, 0]. For i = 1..n, compute the shifted interval (fixed d_i shifts; -1 gives [lo, hi+1]) and intersect with [l_i, r_i]; if empty, print -1.
2. Store R_i for all i. Pick any h_n in R_n.
3. Going backward from i = n: for the allowed steps delta (only d_i if fixed, else 0 and 1), choose one with h_i - delta in R_{i-1}.
4. Set d_i = delta and h_{i-1} = h_i - delta.
5. The intersection with [l_i, r_i] guarantees that every h_i has a valid predecessor, so the backtrack never fails.
complexity: O(n) time per test, O(n) space; sum of n is 2e5
dry_run: Output 0 1 1 1, matching the sample.

brief: Given strings s and t of length n, you may swap any two characters of s whose positions differ by exactly 3 or 4 (k = 3). Decide whether s can be turned into t.
key_idea: Positions joined by differences k and k+1 form connected components via DSU; transpositions along the edges of a connected component generate all its permutations, so s can become t iff each component has the same character multiset in s and t.
solution: 1. Make a DSU over positions 0..n-1.
2. Union i with i+k and i with i+k+1 whenever the index is in range.
3. For each component root r, count letters: add 1 for s[i] and subtract 1 for t[i] in the bucket of root r.
4. Answer YES iff every bucket is all zeros.
5. Edge case: isolated positions (components of size 1) must already match exactly.
complexity: O(n * alpha(n)) time per test, O(n) space; sum of n is 2e5
dry_run: Sample 1: n=6, s=talant, t=atltna. Edges 0-3, 1-4, 2-5, 0-4, 1-5 join all 6 positions into one component.
Letter multiset of s and t are both {a:2, l:1, n:1, t:2}, so YES.
Output YES, matching the sample.

brief: Alice picks k >= 0 and plays k stages on an array; in stage i she must remove an element with value at most k-i+1, and after removal (if the array is non-empty) Bob adds k-i+1 to one element. Find the maximum k that Alice can survive against optimal Bob.
key_idea: Not verified: the fetched text was a paraphrase, and I did not derive a proven greedy for Alice and Bob's optimal play, so no code is given.
solution: 1. Re-read the exact statement on the official page to confirm the rules for Bob's addition.
2. For each candidate k, check Alice's survival with a game analysis that accounts for Bob's best response.
3. Verify any candidate rule against all four sample answers (2, 0, 1, 3) before use.
4. Pick the maximum k that passes; n <= 100 allows an exact check per k.
complexity: unknown until the rule is confirmed
dry_run: Sample a = 1 3 2 1 1 (expected 3): no trace given, since the rule is not confirmed.
No own example is traced for the same reason.

brief: Given strings s and t over letters a, b, c, you may repeatedly swap an adjacent 'ab' into 'ba' or an adjacent 'bc' into 'cb'. Decide whether s can be transformed into t.
key_idea: Letters a and c never pass each other, so the subsequence of non-b letters must match exactly; for each matched letter, the number of b's before it can only increase for a and only decrease for c, and the total b counts must match.
solution: 1. If the count of b in s and t differ, answer NO.
2. Build the list of non-b letters of s with the number of b's before each, and the same for t.
3. If the non-b letter sequences differ, answer NO.
4. For the k-th non-b letter: if it is 'a', require bBefore_t >= bBefore_s; if it is 'c', require bBefore_t <= bBefore_s.
5. Otherwise answer YES.
complexity: O(n) time per test, O(n) space; sum of n is 1e5
dry_run: Sample 4: s=bcaabababc, t=cbbababaac. Non-b letters of s: c(1) a(1) a(1) a(2) a(3) c(4); of t: c(0) a(2) a(3) a(3) a(4) c(4).
Letters match. For a: 2>=1, 3>=1, 3>=2, 4>=3 all hold. For c: 0<=1 and 4<=4 hold.
Output YES, matching the sample.

brief: Two arrays a and b hold the odd numbers and the even numbers from 1 to 2n, respectively. An operation swaps two adjacent elements inside one array. Find the minimum number of swaps so that a is lexicographically smaller than b.
key_idea: a < b is decided by the first elements, which always differ (odd vs even). So choose an odd v in a and an even w in b with v < w, cost = index of v in a + index of w in b, and minimize over pairs using a running minimum of indices.
solution: 1. Store posA[v] for odd v and posB[w] for even w (0-based indices).
2. Scan x = 1..2n. Keep curA = min posA[v] over odd v < x seen so far.
3. At each even x, candidate = curA + posB[x]; take the minimum over all even x.
4. Moving v to the front of a costs posA[v] adjacent swaps; moving w to the front of b costs posB[w] swaps; these choices are independent.
5. Edge case: if no odd value below an even x exists yet, curA stays large and that candidate is ignored by the minimum.
complexity: O(n) time per test, O(n) space; sum of n is 1e5
dry_run: x=2: curA = posA[1] = 2, candidate 2+0 = 2. x=4: curA = min(2, posA[3]=1) = 1, candidate 1+1 = 2. x=6: curA = 1, candidate 1+2 = 3.
Minimum 2, matching the sample.

brief: Vanya needs the average of his n exam grades to reach at least avg. Each exam grade a_i can be raised by 1 point for b_i essays, up to the maximum r. Find the minimum total essays needed.
key_idea: Needed total gain = avg*n - sum(a). Raise the cheapest exams first (sorted by b), each up to its cap r - a_i, until the need is met.
solution: 1. Compute sum of a and need = avg*n - sum. If need <= 0, answer 0.
2. Build pairs (b_i, r - a_i) and sort by b ascending.
3. Walk the sorted list; take min(need, cap_i) points at cost b_i each, reducing need.
4. Stop when need is 0 and print the total cost.
5. Caps are non-negative because a_i <= r; use 64-bit integers since avg*n can be 1e11.
complexity: O(n log n) time per test, O(n) space; n up to 1e5
dry_run: Sample 1: n=5, r=5, avg=4, sum a = 17, need = 3.
Sorted by b: (b=1, cap 2), (b=2, cap 2), (b=2, cap 0), (b=5, cap 1), (b=7, cap 1).
Take 2 at cost 1 each (cost 2), then take 1 at cost 2 (cost 2). Total 4, matching the sample.

brief: DZY has n chemicals and m reacting pairs. He pours them one at a time; the danger doubles when the chemical poured reacts with one already in the tube. Find the maximum final danger over all orders, starting from 1.
key_idea: The answer is 2^(n - c), where c is the number of connected components of the reaction graph: pour each component in BFS order so every chemical except the first of its component doubles.
solution: 1. Use a DSU on the m reacting pairs and count components c (isolated chemicals are components).
2. Upper bound: the first chemical poured from each component cannot double, so at most n - c doublings.
3. Lower bound: pour each component in BFS order; every later chemical has an earlier neighbour, so it doubles.
4. Answer = 2^(n - c) computed with 64-bit integers (the original bound on n is small, around 50; the bound was not visible in the fetch).
complexity: O((n + m) alpha(n)) time, O(n) space
dry_run: Sample 3: n=3, edges 1-2 and 2-3. One component, c=1.
Answer = 2^(3-1) = 4, matching the sample.
Sample 1: n=1, m=0. c=1, answer 2^0 = 1, matching the sample.

brief: Given n boxes with a_i blocks, you may add blocks to any boxes. Then for any chosen box, all its blocks must be moved into the other n-1 boxes so those boxes end with equal counts. Find the minimum number of blocks to add.
key_idea: Let S be the sum and M the maximum. The final common count T must satisfy T >= M and (n-1)*T >= S, so T = max(M, ceil(S/(n-1))), and the answer is (n-1)*T - S.
solution: 1. Compute S = sum of a and M = max of a.
2. Target T = max(M, ceil(S / (n-1))).
3. Each non-chosen box must hold at most T after additions, and the total after additions must equal (n-1)*T so the chosen box's blocks fill exactly the gaps.
4. Answer = (n-1)*T - S, which is non-negative by construction.
5. Use 64-bit integers: (n-1)*T can reach about 1e14.
complexity: O(n) time per test, O(1) extra space; sum of n is 1e5
dry_run: Answer = 2*4 - 7 = 1, matching the sample.
Sample 3: a = 0 3 0, S=3, M=3, n-1=2. ceil(3/2)=2, T = 3. Answer = 2*3 - 3 = 3, matching the sample.

brief: Given an array a of n values in [0, n], for each k from 0 to n count how many distinct MEX values are achievable after removing exactly k elements.
key_idea: MEX = m is achievable after removing k elements iff all of 0..m-1 are present, and cnt[m] <= k <= n - m. So each valid m adds +1 on that interval of k, done with a difference array.
solution: 1. Count cnt[v] for v = 0..n.
2. For m = 0, 1, 2, ...: process m with the interval [cnt[m], n - m] (non-empty when cnt[m] <= n - m).
3. Stop after processing the first m with cnt[m] = 0, since larger m need a missing value below them to be present.
4. Add +1 at the interval start and -1 after its end in a difference array over k.
5. Prefix-sum the difference array; output the values for k = 0..n.
complexity: O(n) time per test, O(n) space; sum of n is 2e5
dry_run: Output 1 3 3 2 1, matching the sample.

brief: On an n x n grid, color some border cells black so the top row has U black cells, the right column R, the bottom row D, and the left column L. Decide whether this is possible.
key_idea: Enumerate the 16 choices of which corner cells are black; each corner counts for two sides, so each side needs its remaining count to fit in its n-2 middle cells.
solution: 1. For each mask of the four corners (TL, TR, BR, BL), compute how many black corners each side gets.
2. For side with requirement c and corner count k, the middle cells must supply rem = c - k, which must satisfy 0 <= rem <= n-2.
3. The answer is YES iff some mask makes all four sides valid.
4. Corner cells are shared, so enumerating masks avoids double counting.
5. Edge case: n = 2 has no middle cells, so each side must be matched exactly by corners.
complexity: O(16) time per test, O(1) space
dry_run: Sample 4: n=2, U=R=D=L=1. Middle length n-2 = 0, so each side needs exactly one black corner.
Mask TL and BR black: top = 1, right = 1, bottom = 1, left = 1, all rem = 0.
Output YES, matching the sample.

brief: Given a sorted array and k, split it into exactly k non-empty contiguous pieces. The cost is the sum over pieces of (max - min). Minimize the total cost.
key_idea: Total cost is (a_n - a_1) minus the sum of the k-1 largest adjacent gaps, since each cut removes one gap from the total; choose the largest gaps as cuts.
solution: 1. Since the array is sorted, a piece's max - min equals the sum of adjacent gaps inside it.
2. Summing over pieces gives total = (a_n - a_1) - (sum of gaps at the k-1 cut positions).
3. Gaps are d_i = a_{i+1} - a_i, i = 1..n-1 (all >= 0).
4. Sort the gaps descending and subtract the first k-1 of them from a_n - a_1.
5. Edge case: k = 1 means no cuts, so the answer is a_n - a_1.
complexity: O(n log n) time per test, O(n) space; n up to 3e5
dry_run: k-1 = 2 largest gaps are 19 and 7, so cost = 38 - 26 = 12, matching the sample.
Sample 2 (k=4): total 6, gaps 2 0 4, subtract 4+2+0 = 6 to get 0, matching.

brief: Given n and x, build the lexicographically smallest permutation p of 1..n with p_1 = x, p_n = 1, and p_i divisible by i for every i < n; print -1 if none exists.
key_idea: Only x | n (or x = n) can work, since the value chain from position x must reach n through divisors. Greedily link x to the smallest divisor of n greater than and divisible by x, then repeat until n; all other positions keep p_i = i.
solution: 1. If x != n and n % x != 0, print -1.
2. Otherwise start with the identity: p_1 = x, p_n = 1, p_i = i for the middle positions.
3. If x != n, let cur = x. While cur != n, find the smallest d in (cur, n] with n % d == 0 and d % cur == 0; set p[cur] = d and cur = d.
4. The chain covers exactly the positions whose values were displaced, so the result is a permutation.
5. Edge case: x = n gives p = n, 2, 3, ..., n-1, 1.
complexity: O(n * number of chain steps) time, at most O(n log n) per test; sum of n is 2e5
dry_run: Sample n=4, x=2: 4 % 2 == 0. Start p = [2, 2, 3, 1]; cur = 2, smallest valid d = 4 (4 | 4, 4 % 2 == 0), so p[2] = 4 and cur = 4.
Result p = 2 4 3 1, matching the sample.
Own example: n=8, x=2: chain 2 -> 4 -> 8 gives p = 2 4 3 8 5 6 7 1.
